candidates.attacker_control: The `from` HTTP request parameter on the `/loginEntry` endpoint is fully attacker-controlled; an attacker can craft a link such as `https://jenkins/loginEntry?from=//attacker.example/phish` and deliver it to an authenticated Jenkins user.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Absolute URLs (`http://evil`, `javascript:`) are rejected by `startsWith("/")`, so exploitation is limited to scheme-relative and slash/backslash-normalization variants. I could not run the server, so I could not observe the emitted Location header or any servlet/Stapler normalization; however, the snapshot itself treats `sendRedirect2(<user value>)` as dangerous unless `Util.isSafeToRedirectTo` passes (DirectoryBrowserSupport.java:164 and ParametersDefinitionProperty.java:177 both carry explicit `avoid open redirect` comments), which is strong in-repo evidence that scheme-relative values reach the browser as external redirects. `AuthenticationProcessingFilter2` (the default login form path) already performs the safe check, so the login form itself is not the vector; the vector is the `/loginEntry` route. The endpoint requires an authenticated principal, lowering exploitability to a phishing/redirect abuse rather than an unauthenticated attack. I did not find any contradicting guard around this specific call site.
candidates.impact: Client-side open redirect after login. Enables phishing (redirect to a look-alike Jenkins login page), credential/token harvesting, and abusing trust in the Jenkins origin (e.g., link/referrer based flows). It does not by itself bypass authentication or authorization and does not execute code; severity is limited but the flaw is a concrete same-origin/domain-check failure at an authentication-adjacent endpoint.
candidates.prerequisites: Jenkins with security enabled (any authorization strategy) and a victim who is already authenticated (the method returns early when `req.getUserPrincipal()==null`). No special permissions beyond being logged in are needed. The javadoc says the method is used by LegacySecurityRealm, but the URL route and principal check are realm-independent; `/loginEntry` is mapped in war/src/main/webapp/WEB-INF/web.xml (security-constraint for authenticated principals).
candidates.root_cause: core/src/main/java/jenkins/model/Jenkins.java:3954-3958 obtains the request parameter `from` and only checks `from.startsWith("/")` before `rsp.sendRedirect2(from)`. A value such as `//attacker.example/...` (protocol/scheme-relative URL) or `http:`-free backslash variants passes that check, is forwarded verbatim to Stapler's `sendRedirect2`, and is resolved by the browser as an external origin, despite the inline comment stating the URL must stay in this domain. The repository already contains the intended validator `hudson.Util.isSafeToRedirectTo` (core/src/main/java/hudson/Util.java:1621-1627, rejects absolute and scheme-relative URIs, used with `// avoid open redirect` comments in hudson/model/DirectoryBrowserSupport.java:164, hudson/model/ParametersDefinitionProperty.java:177, hudson/security/AuthenticationProcessingFilter2.java:56), so the safe helper is available to Jenkins.java (import hudson.*) but is not applied at this sink.
candidates.title: Open redirect via `from` parameter in Jenkins.doLoginEntry (insufficient scheme-relative URL validation before sendRedirect2)
candidates.trace: GET /loginEntry?from=//attacker.example -> Jenkins.doLoginEntry -> `req.getUserPrincipal()` non-null -> `from.startsWith("/")` is true for `//attacker.example` (also true for `/\attacker.example`) -> `rsp.sendRedirect2(from)` -> HTTP 302 with Location `//attacker.example` -> browser treats it as scheme-relative and navigates to the attacker origin.
candidates.unverified: Runtime confirmation was not possible (no build/tests available in the snapshot; test trees and Jelly views are absent). I could not verify that a regression test for this endpoint exists or fails, could not confirm Stapler 1.250.1's exact sendRedirect2 normalization, and cannot confirm that this is the benchmark's ground-truth item — it is submitted as the strongest source-evidenced candidate, not a confirmed exploit.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-601 URL Redirection to Untrusted Site ('Open Redirect')

coverage_summary: Reviewed the source-visible Jenkins core snapshot (8936 files) with read-only tools; the P1 relation index covers the same 8936 files (0 missing, 0 hash mismatches) but is syntactic only (no data flow, reachability, or SAST results), and all index-derived leads were re-verified against source text. The snapshot contains no test sources (core/src/test, test module absent) and no Jelly views or binary assets, so UI-layer sinks and test-confirmed behavior could not be assessed. Areas actually read include: Jenkins/Job/Run/AbstractItem/View/ListView/Computer/SlaveComputer/Queue/User/ItemGroupMixIn/LogRecorder/ParametersAction/BuildAuthorizationToken/LoadStatistics handlers; security realm, filters, CSRF, API tokens, remember-me, and authorization strategies; file/path handling (DirectoryBrowserSupport, FilePath, FilePathFilter, IdStrategy, User migration); XStream2/ConsoleNote/CLI deserialization; Secret/ConfidentialStore/AdminWhitelistRule; URL/redirect sinks (grep for sendRedirect2, new URL, isSafeToRedirectTo, startsWith(\"/\")); CLI modules. Other core areas (install/UpdateCenter/PluginManager internals, remoting-dependent classes, tools/installers, most of jenkins/util, war JS/CSS) were only searched or skimmed, not exhaustively read.
limitations: No code execution, build, tests, or scanners were run; findings are source-evidence-only and not runtime-confirmed.

P1 relation index is navigational/syntactic only (no complete control/data-flow, no semantic resolution, no exploitability proof) and was used only to navigate, then each relevant edge was checked in source.

Test trees and Jelly/binary resources are absent from the visible snapshot, so behavior that depends on views/Jelly (including any permission checks performed there) and any regression tests could not be inspected.

Whether the open-redirect candidate corresponds to the benchmark's ground-truth vulnerability is unknown; ground truth, patches, CVE metadata and sibling runs were not consulted (and were not available).

Stapler 1.250.1 and remoting libraries are external dependencies not present in the snapshot, so sendRedirect2 resolution semantics and JNLP secret routing were inferred from in-repo usage patterns rather than library source.

rejected_leads.lead: hudson/security/csrf/CrumbFilter.java:66-70 — result of the legacy `extractCrumbFromRequest(httpRequest, ".crumb")` compatibility fallback is discarded (`crumb` stays null), so clients using the legacy crumb field name fail CSRF validation.
rejected_leads.reason: This is a functionality regression that fails closed (request is rejected with 403), not a security exposure; no bypass or privilege gain follows from it, and it may be pre-existing upstream behavior.

rejected_leads.lead: jenkins/model/IdStrategy.java:274 (CaseInsensitive.idFromFilename) — `else if ('A' <= c && c <= 'a')` instead of `c <= 'Z'`; characters '['..'`' (including backslash) are retained instead of dropped when converting directory names back to user IDs.
rejected_leads.reason: Reachable only for files already present in $JENKINS_HOME/users (a trusted, admin/filesystem-controlled location); filenameOf() re-sanitizes IDs before any path is built, so I could not construct a remote/attacker-reachable traversal or impersonation path. Weak impact; kept out of the candidate list.

rejected_leads.lead: hudson/model/DirectoryBrowserSupport.java:169-174 — the traversal guard (`path.replace('\\','/').indexOf("/../")!=-1`) does not reject a path ending in `/..` (e.g. `/..`) or `/foo/..`, allowing `root.child("../index.html")` to be served.
rejected_leads.reason: Escape depth is one level and limited to the fixed index file name (default `index.html`) or directory listing, so impact is marginal and it appears to be long-standing upstream behavior rather than the injected/reverted security fix.

rejected_leads.lead: hudson/slaves/SlaveComputer.java:174-176 — public getter `getJnlpMac()` returns the agent secret HMAC with no permission check or annotation; if Stapler exposes it as /computer/<name>/jnlpMac, any user able to reach the computer object could obtain the agent secret and connect a rogue agent.
rejected_leads.reason: Potentially critical if HTTP-reachable, but I could not verify from the available files that the getter is routed or which permission governs the route (the SlaveComputer/Computer Jelly views and test trees are not part of the snapshot; soJnlpMac-style checks may exist in excluded views or the remoting library). Flagged as an unconfirmed lead, not the submitted candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: hudson/cli/CliCrumbExclusion.java:44-50 — all requests whose pathInfo is `/cli` are excluded from CSRF validation; also BasicAuthenticationFilter accepts API tokens as Basic-auth passwords.
rejected_leads.reason: Both are deliberate, documented upstream designs (JENKINS-18114; API-token auth requires the per-user token over a per-request credential), and I found no missing validation that turns them into an exploitable CSRF/auth bypass in this snapshot.

summary: Snapshot is Jenkins core at version 2.73.4-SNAPSHOT (stable-2.73, post-2.73.3, ~Oct 2017), 8936 text-source files (tests, Jelly views and binary assets are not present in the snapshot). I reviewed the security-critical core paths: web request handlers and permission checks (Jenkins, Job, Run, AbstractItem, View/ListView, Computer/SlaveComputer, ItemGroupMixIn, Queue, User, LogRecorder, ParameterizedJobMixIn, BuildAuthorizationToken), authentication/authorization (HudsonFilter, SecurityRealm, AuthenticationProcessingFilter2, BasicAuthenticationFilter, ApiTokenProperty, remember-me, CsrfFilter/CrumbIssuer), path/file handling (DirectoryBrowserSupport, FilePath/FilePathFilter, IdStrategy/User), serialization (XStream2, ConsoleNote, Connection), and crypto/secret handling (Secret, DefaultConfidentialStore, AdminWhitelistRule, TokenBasedRememberMeServices2). One issue meets the evidence threshold: the `from` parameter used by `Jenkins.doLoginEntry` is validated only with `startsWith("/")`, which accepts scheme-relative URLs such as `//evil.com` and is then passed to `sendRedirect2` as-is — an open redirect (CWE-601) that contradicts both the method's own comment ("make sure the URL falls into this domain") and the repo's own `Util.isSafeToRedirectTo` helper used for exactly this purpose at three other redirect sinks. Other anomalies I found are fail-closed or too weak/unverifiable to submit.
